title: Shinya Yamanaka (1962–, 2012 Nobel & 2009 Lasker) — 'Mr. Obstacle,' Four Hundred Mouse Cages, and the Four Factors of iPSCs

teenKit.tldr: A clumsy young surgeon nicknamed "Mr. Obstacle" quit the operating room, pivoted to research, and figured out how to turn regular skin cells back into universal stem cells using just four genetic factors—winning a Nobel Prize while struggling to fix his own washing machine.
teenKit.whyItMatters: This breakthrough means scientists can theoretically grow any human tissue in a lab to cure degenerative diseases, testing treatments without ever using human embryos.
keyTakeaways: Failing miserably at one path (like surgery) doesn't mean you're useless; it might just mean you're on the wrong terrain and need to retreat to find your true strengths.
Major scientific breakthroughs often come from following weird anomalies and brute-forcing a solution rather than waiting for a neat, elegant theory.
True innovation relies on radical openness and teamwork, treating science like a relay race where everyone builds on each other's efforts.

vocab.meaning: A harmless, benign fatty lump that grows just beneath the skin.
A blank-slate cell that has the potential to develop into many different cell types in the body.
A common type of cell found in connective tissue, frequently used in lab experiments because they are easy to grow.
A traditional Japanese long-distance relay race where runners pass a sash to symbolize teamwork and shared effort.

quiz.question: Why did senior surgeons at Osaka National Hospital call Shinya Yamanaka "Jamanaka" or "Mr. Obstacle"?
options: He constantly argued with the hospital director about budget cuts.
He froze up during routine surgeries, fumbling tools and slowing down the entire hospital schedule.
He refused to wash his hands before entering the operating room.
He kept stealing lab equipment to run unauthorized experiments.
quiz.explanation: Yamanaka struggled terribly with physical surgical skills as a rookie resident, earning a mocking nickname before leaving clinical practice for research.

quiz.question: What household chore was Yamanaka struggling with at the exact moment he received the call from Stockholm about the Nobel Prize?
options: Fixing a violently rattling washing machine with a screwdriver
Unclogging a stubborn kitchen sink drain
Ripping out old carpets in his hallway
quiz.explanation: In a great contrast to winning the world's highest scientific honor, Yamanaka was down on his knees trying to fix a broken washing machine.

quiz.question: Which of the following best describes Yamanaka's overarching approach to handling skepticism and scientific failure?
options: Hiding his mistakes until he could publish a flawless paper
Suing rival labs that doubted his cell reprogramming data
Weaponizing radical openness and sharing his raw data to crush doubters
Quitting science entirely whenever an experiment failed
quiz.explanation: Yamanaka famously disarmed skeptics by sharing everything openly and adopting a humble, team-oriented mindset.
